name: S. B. Cobb's Saddle, Harness and Trunk Manufactory
aka: Goss & Cobb, saddle and harness makers

documented_range.note:
THE SURVIVAL THIS RECORD ASKED FOR IS NOW READ, AND THE RANGE MOVES OFF `reconstructed` FOR IT. The note this replaces closed with the sentence "TO RESOLVE: further issues of the Chicago Democrat or the Chicago American. One line of an 1834 or 1835 advertisement would settle the survival and might settle the corner." The Chicago American carries three such lines, and they settle the first half of that and not the second.

WHAT IS PRINTED. The Democrat of 26 November 1833 opens the range over the firm's own name: 'they have opened a shop in this village, on the conner of Lake and Canal-streets' (the 'conner' is the page's). The American then sets the same trading card three times in the weeks either side of the scene date — 1835-06-08 p3 c5 (`chicago_american_1835_06_08#c007`), 1835-06-13 p3 c6 (`chicago_american_1835_06_13#c016`) and 1835-07-11 p2 c1 (`chicago_american_1835_07_11#c008`) — reading, in the second and clearest of them, '[S]A[D]DLE, HARNESS & TRUNK M[anufa]c[tor]y. S[. ]B[. ]COB[B] [w]il[l] [c]o[nt]in[ue] the [above business] at his shop, corner [o]f [… ][st]re[et]s'. The last of the three is dated ten days AFTER 1 July 1835.

WHY `inferred` AND NOT `attested`, WHICH IS THE WHOLE OF WHAT IS BEING CLAIMED. That the saddlery trade was carried on at a corner of Lake Street in the first week of July 1835 is printed. That it was carried on in THIS BUILDING is reasoned: the same trade, one of the same two partners, the words 'will continue the above business AT HIS SHOP', and Lake Street named in all four printings. The American never resolves the cross street — 'Lake anc Amor. streets', then no street names at all, then 'corner of Lake and THE Balle' — so the corner is still the Democrat's and the identification of the two shops is an argument rather than a statement. T-0305 holds that cross street open on the page images.

THE `to` DATE IS UNCHANGED AND IS STILL HOUSEKEEPING: 1835-12-31 is the end of the scene year, not a closure. Nothing dates an end. What has changed is that the nineteen-month gap the old note carried forward on nothing is now bridged by four printed dates, the last of them past the scene date.

change_note: The shop as the Democrat's advertisement opens it in November 1833 and as the American's three printings carry it to July 1835 — the same premises, the same trade, and one proprietor instead of two. NOTHING ABOUT THE BUILDING CHANGES ON THIS RECORD: the position, the footprint and the form are exactly what they were, and the American resolves none of them. What changes is the range's grade and the name over the door.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE JUNCTION IS SELF-REPORTED IN A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT, WHICH IS AS GOOD AS AN ADDRESS GETS IN THIS DATASET, AND THE QUADRANT IS THIS RECORD'S GUESS. The advertisement says 'on the conner of Lake and Canal-streets' and, exactly as with the Democrat's own imprint at South Water and Clark, that settles the JUNCTION and not which of the four corners. The north-east corner is taken by the Green Tree Tavern (data/structures/green_tree_tavern.json), which leaves three; the south-east is adopted, which is a one-in-three choice and a roughly 40 m error if it is wrong. METHOD: the modern West Lake Street / North Canal Street intersection centre is EPSG:26916 E 446913.03, N 4637287.42 - the same OpenStreetMap node this project uses as ground control point G5 on the Wright 1834 fit, and the best-fitting of the eight at 1.8 m residual. The building's north face is set on the Lake Street frontage 12.2 m south of that centre and its west face on the Canal frontage 12.2 m east of it, 12.2 m being half of an 80 ft street as annotated on Hathaway 1834; the stored coordinate is the polygon origin AFTER the 180 degree facade bearing, which under the renderer's convention (renderers/web/js/walker.js) puts it at the building's north-east corner. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (data/datum.json, 17.5 m RMS), plus the quadrant. A LARGER AND ONE-DIRECTIONAL RESIDUAL IS INHERITED FROM THE GREEN TREE'S RECORD AND IS RESTATED HERE RATHER THAN HIDDEN: 'Canal Street' in 1833 may mean the street a block back from the river, where the modern node is, or the riverbank street then called West Water and now Canal. If the advertisement means the bank street, this shop belongs about 145 m east. The same doubt sits on the Green Tree at the same crossing, and settling one settles both. Facade bearing 180, north onto Lake Street, inferred from the street rather than from any statement.
placement.symbolic_location: The corner of Lake Street and Canal Street (historically Lake and West Water), west bank; placed on the SOUTH-EAST quadrant of the crossing - south side of Lake, east side of Canal - fronting north onto Lake.

footprint.note: INVENTED. The advertisement gives a trade, a corner and a stock list and no dimension. 9.144 x 6.096 m is 30 x 20 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated per data/datum.json's units rule - the same size this project gives Frederick Thomas's shop on South Water Street, kept deliberately rather than replaced with a fresh guess, on the reasoning docs/LIBERTIES.md L29 states about the bridge's pier spacing: a new number would look like a finding and would not be one. WHAT THE ADVERTISEMENT DOES IMPLY, without measuring anything: the firm kept saddles, harness, bridles and trunks 'on hand', manufactured to order, and trimmed 'Coaches, Chaises and Waggons', which is a shop with a workroom behind it and enough door to get a waggon at least alongside. That argues for the larger end of a shop rather than a stall, and it is an argument, not a measurement.

stories.note: NOT ATTESTED. One storey is the ordinary form for a village shop opened in 1833 and it is what this project gives the other trades advertised in the same issue. Chosen rather than derived.

construction.note: Not attested for this building. Frame is the reading for a shop 'opened' in the village in the autumn of 1833: the town had sawn lumber and carpenters by then, and Silas B. Cobb - who is almost certainly the Cobb of this firm - is named by DRLOIH as the carpenter who built the Green Tree Tavern at this very corner earlier the same year. Braced rather than balloon is the conservative reading for 1833, when balloon framing in Chicago was one or two years old. The distinction changes stud rhythm behind the sheathing and is not visible at this level of detail.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 3.0 m is about 10 ft to the plate - a single storey of shop with headroom over a counter, and a little more than the 8 1/2 ft this project gives a log dwelling of the same date. What is inferred is that the wall height falls in this range, not that it is exactly 3.0 m.

roof_type.note: Not attested for this building. Gable is the near-universal roof form for a small frame building of this type, period and region.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 33 degrees is this archetype's mid-range for a small frame shop, inferred from construction practice rather than measured - the same value this project uses for the other Democrat-advertised shops.

chimneys.note: Not attested. One stack is the minimum a workroom heated through a Chicago winter needed, and a saddler works with wax, thread and hot irons. The COUNT is the inference; position, size and material are the archetype's - docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 4.5 in — dealt by tools/deal_siding_stock.py: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention.

function.note: Verbatim from the page, read from the scan on 2026-08-11: '[Saddle & H]arness Making. GOSS & COBB, respectfully inform the inhabitants of Chicago and the neighboring settlements, that they have opened a shop in this village, on the conner of Lake and Canal-streets, where they have on hand and will manufacture to order, Ladies' and Gentlemens SADDLES, Brass, Silver and Common Mounted HARNESS, Bridles; Martingales, &c. &c. Hard leather and common TRUNKS. Coaches, Chaises and Waggons Trimmed in [best] style. Repairing immediately attended to when brought to their shop. N.B. By strict attention to business, they hope for a share of patronage.' Andreas's summary of the same advertising columns carries 'Goss & Cobb, saddle and harness making' and adds nothing. THE ENGRAVING OF A SADDLE ABOVE THE ADVERTISEMENT IS A PRINTER'S STOCK CUT and no fact about this shop or its goods may be read out of it - the same rule data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json sets for the building cut over 'Two Buildings to Let'. THE AMERICAN WIDENS THE TRADE BY ONE WORD AND CORRECTS ITSELF DOING IT. Its three 1835 printings of Cobb's card head the same shop 'SADDLE, HARNESS & TRUNK MANUFACTORY' — trunks were already in the 1833 list of goods ('Hard leather and common TRUNKS') and are now in the heading. The first of the three, 1835-06-08 p3 c5, sets that heading as 'LB, HA & TRUNK M' and was read in this corpus as a HAT manufactory before 1835-06-13 p3 c6 set it legibly over the same name; the misreading is left standing in that issue's extraction file rather than quietly swapped. The function VALUE does not move — a saddlery and harness shop that also made trunks in 1833 is the same trade in 1835 — and the grade does not move either; what the American adds is a second, independent witness three weeks either side of the scene date.

occupants.value: S. B. Cobb, saddle, harness and trunk manufacturer
occupants.note:
THE FIRM THAT OPENED THIS SHOP WAS DISSOLVED FOUR AND A HALF MONTHS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, AND THE PAPER THAT PRINTS THE DISSOLUTION PRINTS WHO CARRIED ON. The Chicago American runs the notice in its first two issues — `chicago_american_1835_06_08#c006` and `chicago_american_1835_06_13#c015`, the second legible where the first is not: 'NOTICE. [Th]e co-partnership heretofore [existing under] the firm of Go[ss] & Cob[b] [is] this day [dis]solved by m[ut]ual consent. OL[IVE]R GOS[S]. S. B. [C]O[BB]. Chicago, Feb. 18, 183[5].' Beside it, in the same issue, Cobb's own card: 'S[. ]B[. ]COB[B] [w]il[l] [c]o[nt]in[ue] the [above business] at his shop' (`chicago_american_1835_06_13#c016`). A dissolution dated 18 February and still running in June is ordinary; what is not ordinary is having both halves of it — the end of the partnership and the survivor's continuation — set on the same page.

SO ON 1 JULY 1835 THIS IS COBB'S SHOP AND NOT THE FIRM'S, and the record says so on the attribute rather than in a footnote. The firm name is kept in `aka` and in the range's own note, because it is what opened the building and what the Democrat's 1833 advertisement attests; deleting it would lose the better-attested of the two facts to record the later one.

WHAT IS STILL NOT SETTLED. The initials are completed to 'S. B. Cobb' by the firm name and by his own signed card, and the corpus mints him as a person on that card and not on the dissolution notice. Whether he is the Silas B. Cobb whom DRLOIH names as the carpenter who built the Green Tree Tavern on the opposite corner of this same crossing in 1833 is STILL NOT ESTABLISHED HERE — no source reached connects the saddler to the carpenter in terms, and the American does not either. Oliver Goss's forename, which this record could not read before, is printed in the 1835-06-13 setting of the notice.

residents.name: The Goss and Cobb household
residents.why: The firm names itself and its corner in its own advertisement.

persons.name: O. Goss
persons.note: THE FORENAME IS A GUESS AT AN INITIAL AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. The advertisement gives 'Goss' with no initial. Andreas's table of first purchasers of canal lots carries an 'O. Goss, Washington Co. Vermont' buying on 3 September 1832, which is the only Goss in the volume near this date and place, and this record adopts that initial while grading the person derived because the identification is a reading and not a statement. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later.

persons.name: Silas B. Cobb
persons.note: IDENTIFIED, NOT PROVEN, AND ALREADY FLAGGED IN THE STRUCTURES LAYER. data/structures/goss_cobb_saddlery.json says in terms: 'Neither source connects the saddler to the carpenter in terms, so the identification is not made.' This household makes it, one grade down, because a minor arriving on 1 June 1833 and a Cobb advertising at Lake and Canal that November is a coherent single person and because leaving the initial unresolved loses a dated arrival. THE GRADE IS THE WARNING and a source that separates the two men should split this record. OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Cobb, Silas B. | 1833, May 29, | Montpelier, Vt. | 67 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Silas B. Cobb” (f1839_v0352, printed page 43, ward 2, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Cobb' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins S. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. FERGUS 1839'S FORT DEARBORN ADDITION LOT SALE — JUNE 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. This person bid at the sale of the Fort Dearborn Addition, 10-24 June 1839, printed in Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 at pages 47-49. The bidder is printed as “S. B. Cobb”. 2 lot rows, $516.0 in all: block 10 lot 10 at $268.5 (f1839_lot0183, printed page 49); block 10 lot 11 at $247.5 (f1839_lot0184, printed page 49). The sale table's own shorthand, recorded and not flattened: 1 of those rows prints the bidder as a ditto mark under the name above rather than the name itself; 2 carry the block number forward from the last row that printed one. What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago between the 10th and the 24th of June 1839 and bid at the Fort Dearborn Addition sale. It is written as 1839 evidence with describes_date 1839-06, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a land sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. THE LOT IS NOT A LOCATION FOR 1835: the Fort Dearborn Addition is the Beaubien, or Reservation, lands, which in July 1835 were the garrison's ground and were not platted into lots at all. It places no house, no shop and no household in the town this project builds. No trade, no address in the town of 1835, no household and no house. The block and lot are the only location on the page, they are ground platted in 1839 out of the garrison's reservation, and they place nobody in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Cobb' folds to the same string as the bidder's, and the given name of both begins S. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_lots_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a lot sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Cobb, Stephen A, | Profession. | April 3, 1889.” (second_presb_0120, printed page 160), admitted 1889-04-03 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Cobb' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins S. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

residents.research_note: SADDLERY IS THE TRADE THAT PROVES THE TOWN HAD TRAFFIC. Two saddle and harness makers advertising at Lake and Canal in 1833 - on the west side, on the road out of town - is evidence about wagons, teams and the overland trade that this dataset otherwise sees only through Ordinance 9's barrels in the street. THIS HOUSEHOLD MAKES AN IDENTIFICATION THE STRUCTURES LAYER DECLINED TO MAKE, one grade down and with the disagreement written on both persons; that asymmetry is deliberate and should be read as the residents layer proposing a reading, not as the dataset having changed its mind.

research_note:
A LAKE STREET BUILDING THAT EXISTS BECAUSE ITS OWNERS PAID TO SAY WHERE IT WAS. Of everything this parcel looked at, this is the only address that comes from the town describing itself in its own week rather than from a compilation written fifty years later - and it is a better positional statement than most records in this dataset hold, because an advertiser's customers had to be able to find him. What it cannot do is carry the building nineteen months forward to the scene date, or say anything at all about its size, its material or its shape. So the range WAS conjectural (see the last paragraph of this note, which is where it stopped being so), the footprint is conjectural, the storey count is conjectural, and what survives of the evidence in the mesh is a small frame shop of about the right kind at about the right crossing. TWO GUARDS. (1) THE QUADRANT: the advertisement says 'the conner of Lake and Canal-streets' and names no side, exactly as the Democrat's own imprint says 'on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets' and names none. The Green Tree Tavern holds the north-east corner of this crossing, so three remain and this record picks the south-east. (2) THE STREET ITSELF: 'Canal' at this crossing carries the doubt already recorded on the Green Tree - modern Canal Street lies a full block back from the west bank, where the 1830s riverbank street was West Water, and if the advertisement means the bank street this shop belongs about 145 m east. That doubt is worth more here than the quadrant, and the check that would settle both is the lot geometry on Wright 1834 or Hathaway 1834. THE SADDLE ENGRAVING OVER THE ADVERTISEMENT IS A STOCK CUT and nothing may be read out of it.

WHAT THE CHICAGO AMERICAN ADDED, 2026-08-29. This record used to close by naming the two things that would move it: further issues of either 1835 paper, to settle the survival and perhaps the corner. Both questions were put to the American's thirteen issues and it answers one. SURVIVAL: yes, and past the scene date — the trade is advertised at a corner of Lake Street on 8 June, 13 June and 11 July 1835, so the nineteen-month carry-forward the old range rested on is now bridged and the range is graded `inferred`. THE CORNER: no — the cross street is lost in all three printings ('Lake anc Amor. streets', no street names at all, 'corner of Lake and THE Balle'), so the quadrant guard below stands exactly as written and the building has not moved a metre. WHAT IT ADDED THAT WAS NOT ASKED FOR: the partnership was dissolved on 18 February 1835 and S. B. Cobb continued alone, which is why the name over this door, and the board on its wall, are his and not the firm's at the scene date.
